summary: Defines a specific mechanism for adding a digitally signed authenticated identity body to a SIP request, building on the S/MIME body idea from RFC 3261. It provides integrity and authentication properties for header information.

eli5.summary: A call setup message can carry a signed note proving who sent it and that the details were not changed on the way.

questions: what is a sip authenticated identity body
what headers must an aib contain
how does sip prevent aib replay
subtitle: A small signed slice of a SIP request that lets the receiver check who really sent it.

tldr.problem: The From header of a SIP request can usually be set to anything, yet many phones show it as caller ID. Signing a full copy of the request is heavy, and many headers legitimately change in transit.
tldr.mechanism: An Authenticated Identity Body (AIB) is a signed message/sipfrag MIME body that carries just enough headers (From, Date, Call-ID and Contact, ideally also To and CSeq) to prove the sender's identity and tie it to the request.
tldr.outcome: A receiver verifies the signature, compares the signer's identity with the From domain, and reports any mismatch to the user. Date and Call-ID checks block replayed AIBs.

today: RFC 3893 is a Proposed Standard, published in September 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Identity Needs a Signature
sections.content:
In SIP, the From header carries a URI such as sip:alice@example.com and an optional display name. A user agent can usually set it arbitrarily, so it gives no assurance that the sender may claim that identity. Still, many user agents show it as a kind of caller ID.

RFC 3261 already lets a sender sign a tunneled message/sip body that copies the request headers. The catch is size and noise: the copy is large, many of its headers are irrelevant to identity, and some change in transit for valid reasons, so the receiver must work out which changes were legitimate.

This RFC proposes a middle path based on message/sipfrag ( RFC 3420 ): sign just enough headers to establish the sender's identity and correlate it with the request. It says the AIB format should be used instead of the tunneled message/sip mechanism to provide the caller's identity. If integrity over other, unrelated headers is needed, message/sip should still be used.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write any name on the front of an envelope. A signed note inside the envelope proves the name is real, and it only needs to hold a few key facts instead of a copy of the whole letter.

sections.title: The AIB Format
sections.content:
An AIB is a MIME body of type message/sipfrag. It MUST have a Content-Disposition disposition-type of aib, a new value defined here. The Content-Disposition header SHOULD also carry a handling parameter showing the body is optional, so a server that does not support AIBs can still process the request.

For an INVITE, the AIB MUST contain From, Date, Call-ID and Contact, and SHOULD also contain To and CSeq. It MAY include other headers that help identify the transaction or give reference integrity.

Unsigned AIBs MUST be treated like AIBs that fail validation. Once signed, the AIB SHOULD be added to the request's existing MIME bodies (such as SDP), turning the outermost body into multipart/mixed if needed.
sections.eli5: The note is a short list of facts about the call, stamped with a special label that says it is an identity note. Once it is signed, it is tucked into the envelope next to the other papers.

sections.title: A Request Carrying an AIB
sections.content:
The RFC shows a full INVITE from Alice to Bob. Its body is multipart/mixed with two parts: an SDP session description, and a multipart/signed part. That signed part uses protocol application/pkcs7-signature with micalg=sha1 and holds the AIB plus a base64 S/MIME signature (smime.p7s).

The AIB repeats From, To, Contact, Date, Call-ID and CSeq from the request, so the signature binds the identity to that particular call attempt.
sections.eli5: Alice's call request holds two things: the details of the call, and a sealed note that repeats a few of those details and proves they came from Alice.

sections.title: Third Parties, Non-INVITE Requests and Responses
sections.content:
Third parties. Some flows, such as REFER and third-party call control (3PCC), involve a third party before an INVITE is sent. A supplemental AIB might carry that party's identity, alongside the regular one. But in those cases the Call-ID, CSeq, To and From of the original request do not match the later INVITE, so correlating an AIB is much harder. The RFC leaves this to further specification work.

Non-INVITE requests. Requests within a dialog generally parallel the INVITE: From, Call-ID, Date and Contact are REQUIRED. New methods or extensions that use AIB security MUST state any special identity requirements in their own Security Considerations.

Responses. A response needs a freshly built AIB. Its From MUST be the responder's address-of-record, NOT the From of the request, and the request's To MUST NOT be included. New Date and Contact headers are generated, while Call-ID and CSeq are copied from the request.
sections.eli5: Replies get their own new sealed note that says who is answering. Special cases like passing a call along to someone else are left for later work.

sections.title: Receiving an AIB
sections.content:
A user agent that receives a request with an AIB MUST verify the signature, including validating the signer's certificate. It then compares the signer's identity (the subjectAltName) with the domain part of the URI in the request's From. They should correspond exactly. If they do not, the agent MUST report this to its user before proceeding. It MAY distinguish minor variations (example.com versus sip.example.com) from major ones (example.com versus example.org) when reporting.

The Date, Call-ID and Contact checks from the Security Considerations MUST also be performed, and any discrepancy MUST be reported to the user.

When the original sender gets a response with an AIB, it SHOULD compare the AIB's From with the original To of its request. If they differ, it SHOULD show the responder's identity to its user. That is not necessarily an attack, since normal re-targeting may send the request elsewhere.
sections.eli5: The receiver checks the seal, then checks that the name on the seal matches the name on the envelope. If something looks off, it tells the person instead of quietly going ahead.

sections.title: Encrypting the Identity
sections.content:
Entities that support S/MIME signatures often support S/MIME encryption too, as described in RFC 3261, Section 23.4.3. Encrypting an AIB keeps it private so that only a key holder can read it. The security then depends on distributing that key safely. The RFC notes the single key could be spread across a network of hosts under common policies, which some telephone networks might require.

When an AIB is encrypted, it SHOULD be encrypted before it is signed. Implementations MUST still accept AIBs that were signed and then encrypted. The RFC's example wraps the message/sipfrag in an application/pkcs7-mime enveloped-data part inside the signed container.
sections.eli5: You can also put the note in a locked box so only people with the right key can read it, and then seal the box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The identity lives in the AIB's From; a valid one is suitable to display as caller ID. The other headers exist to detect replay and cut-and-paste attacks. Leaving them out loses important security properties.

Replay. Implementations MUST follow the Date acceptance rules of RFC 3261, Section 23.4.2 (suggested window: a Date within 3600 seconds of receipt). They MUST also record the Call-IDs seen in AIBs for at least one Date interval (3600 seconds). A replay inside the window fails on duplicate Call-ID, and a replay after it fails on stale Date.

Contact. It ties the AIB to the device that made the request. An attacker who pastes the AIB into their own request would not receive SIP requests meant for that Contact.

To and CSeq. These help but suit not every use. CSeq gives per-transaction replay protection if a new AIB is issued for each transaction, while reusing one AIB for a whole dialog reduces load on the signer. Including To helps spot an AIB re-used to impersonate the sender to a different destination.
sections.eli5: The extra details in the note make it useless to a thief. A copied note is too old, was already used, or points to the real sender's phone, so the thief never gets the answers.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC defines one new MIME Content-Disposition disposition-type value, aib. It is reserved for MIME bodies that contain an authenticated identity, as described in the format section above.
sections.eli5: The RFC asks for one new official label, aib, to be kept just for these identity notes.

data.title: Example AIB
data.code:
Content-Type: message/sipfrag
Content-Disposition: aib; handling=optional

From: Alice <sip:alice@example.com>
To: Bob <sip:bob@example.net>
Contact: <sip:alice@pc33.example.com>
Date: Thu, 21 Feb 2002 13:02:03 GMT
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710
CSeq: 314159 INVITE
